## Current State

`/claude-tweaks:docs-health` filed #2785 proposing specific replacement text for a dangling
commit-hash citation ("squashed into `15553cf`", "`41dc8424f` is not a resolvable object in
this repository"). #2785's own build phase, running a full (unshallowed) history fetch, found
both claims in the *proposed replacement* itself were wrong: `41dc8424f` is a real commit
(just unreachable from `main`), and `15553cf` never touches the files in question — the
actual landing commit is `cdb32b046`. The record had to be fixed against its own proposed fix
text, not just its originally-flagged problem.

## Deliverables

`docs-health`'s staleness-finding procedure for a dangling-commit-hash finding should run (or
instruct the filing pass to run) a full/unshallowed `git log`/`git branch -r --contains` check
against the proposed replacement commit hash(es) before filing — the same check #2785's build
phase had to redo independently — so a filed record's "Proposed" text is not itself stale on
arrival.

## Acceptance Criteria

A dangling-commit-hash staleness finding `docs-health` files includes a replacement citation
that has already been verified reachable (or explicitly marked unresolvable) against full
repo history, not just the shallow-clone view available at filing time.

**Doc:** docs/releasing.md | **Id:** releasing | **Section:** After the merge: which release carried it | **Category:** staleness | **Misleads:** coding agent | **Classification:** additive | **Confidence:** med

Verified-as-of: 9e7cee5dc92cfe8e4b7a431f1ad6aead907e2250

## Current State

docs/releasing.md says 'Unchanged — `_shared/pr-first-merge-post-merge.md` Step 4.1 answers this from tag ancestry alone' and then shows only `git describe --tags --contains --first-parent --match 'v*' <merge-sha>`. The canonical source it cites (plugin/skills/_shared/pr-first-merge-post-merge.md lines 24-27) shows `git fetch origin {integration-branch}` immediately before that same `git describe` line, and explicitly explains why: 'Read it after the merge is confirmed and after the fetch above — a sibling session's tag can land while this PR is being merged.' That race is not hypothetical — the same file cites #603/#678 as the incident that motivated this step. A reader (especially an agent doing a literal copy-paste rather than following the cross-reference) who runs docs/releasing.md's snippet as shown risks a stale/incorrect 'not yet in a release' verdict if a sibling session's tag landed moments earlier and was never fetched locally.

## Deliverables

**Current:**
````
```
git describe --tags --contains --first-parent --match 'v*' <merge-sha>
```
````

**Proposed:**
````
```
git fetch origin <integration-branch>
git describe --tags --contains --first-parent --match 'v*' <merge-sha>
```
````

## Acceptance Criteria

The code block under 'After the merge: which release carried it' in docs/releasing.md includes `git fetch origin <integration-branch>` before the `git describe` command, matching the full command sequence in `plugin/skills/_shared/pr-first-merge-post-merge.md` Step 4.1, which the doc claims to mirror unchanged.

## Release Note

No user-visible change — documentation accuracy fix.

Origin: reflect full (multi-spec batch) from #2633/#2664

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

At the start of run 2026-09-30T190052-spec-2633-2664, `flow-preflight` classified the freshly minted run dir as adoption **case 3** (an adopted, already-running run), not case 2 (a fresh mint).

The cause was the issue-claim step, which had already appended its claim-log lines to `decisions.md`. The preflight treated a non-empty `decisions.md` as evidence of a prior run. The executor ruled case 2 by hand and logged the ruling.

A case-3 misclassification would have triggered the case-3 adoption-recovery backfill (`flow/steps-and-gates.md`) on a run that had nothing to recover.

## Deliverables

1. The preflight's case classification ignores `decisions.md` entries written by the claim step, recognized by their claim-log section or line shape, when deciding fresh vs adopted.
2. Add a regression test with a run dir whose `decisions.md` holds only claim-log lines.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A run dir with only claim-log lines in `decisions.md` classifies as case 2.
- A run dir with any non-claim decision entry still classifies as it does today.

## Release Note

Freshly started /flow runs are no longer mistaken for resumed ones after claiming their records.

Origin: reflect hindsight from #2664

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

Four readers each carry their own copy of the multi-spec "per-spec run dir falls back to its parent for the shared worktree/PR stamps" rule:

- `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/pack.js` `resolveState` (#1930 review C1) — fills `worktree`/`pr` from the parent.
- `plugin/bin/lib/wrap-up/engine-verify.js` `resolvePrNumber` — reads the parent `run-state.json` when the per-spec one is absent (a different rule: whole-file fallback, not per-field).
- `plugin/bin/lib/pr-bookkeeping/precondition.js` `checkPrBookkeepingPrecondition` (#2664) — per-field fill of `worktree`/`pr`/`prExempt` plus the parent `decisions.md` degrade line.
- `plugin/skills/flow/multispec-review-console.md:88` — prose: reads `pr` on the parent `run-state.json`.

The three code copies already disagree on semantics (per-field fill vs whole-file fallback; `/^spec-/` basename gate in two, none in `resolvePrNumber`; `prExempt` honored in one). A fifth reader will copy whichever it finds first.

## Deliverables

1. One exported helper beside `readRunState` in `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/context.js` (e.g. `readRunStateWithParent(runDir)`) implementing the per-field fill for `worktree`/`pr`/`prExempt` behind the `/^spec-/` basename gate, returning `{ state, parentRunDir }`.
2. Migrate `pack.js` `resolveState`, `engine-verify.js` `resolvePrNumber`, and `precondition.js` to it; keep each call site's existing tests green.
3. `resolvePrNumber`'s whole-file fallback converges on the per-field rule (a per-spec `run-state.json` carrying only `status` must still find the parent PR) — add a test for that shape.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `grep -rn "path.dirname(runDir), 'run-state.json'" plugin/bin` returns no hits outside the new helper.
- A per-spec dir with a status-only `run-state.json` resolves the parent PR in all three consumers (one test each).
- `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

No user-visible change — internal consolidation of how multi-spec pipeline runs locate their shared worktree and PR.

## Current State

`needsBackstop` (`plugin/bin/lib/issues/acceptance.js`) returns true for any CLOSED, non-sub-issue
record with no `demo:*` label, and `_shared/github-pr-scan-acceptance.md`'s acceptance-gap fetch
never reads `stateReason`. Against this repo on 2026-09-30: 653 records closed in the last 30 days,
581 classified as gaps — 392 COMPLETED, 188 NOT_PLANNED, 1 DUPLICATE. A not-planned or duplicate
closure has nothing to accept, so roughly a third of the rows are noise; the remaining 392 still
dwarf the 284 `demo:approved` records ever labelled, so the scope cannot converge and its
per-record `/claude-tweaks:demo #N` recommendation is not actionable at this volume. The fetch
also hit its `backlog-fetch-limit` (1000), so its own truncation warning fired.

Evidence: tidy run 2026-09-30T172538-tidy-standalone, scan/acceptance.txt.

## Deliverables

- Exclude `stateReason` NOT_PLANNED and DUPLICATE from `needsBackstop` (fetch `stateReason` in the
  acceptance-gap `gh issue list`), with the same change on the local-files Shape 8 path.
- Decide and document whether health-sweep (`by:*-health`) and capture-only records need a
  disposition at all, or whether the backstop should scope to records a build actually shipped.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A NOT_PLANNED closed record with no `demo:*` label is not a gap; a COMPLETED one still is.
- Unit tests in the acceptance.js suite cover both reasons.

## Release Note

Tidy stops flagging records closed as not-planned or duplicate as missing an acceptance decision.

Origin: /claude-tweaks:tidy run 2026-09-30T172538-tidy-standalone (approved Step 6 Capture)

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`plugin/skills/_shared/github-pr-scan.md:218` (origin/main), item 10 (Unsettled run), fetches
`gh pr list --state all --json number,url,closingIssuesReferences,comments,commits --limit 200`.
GitHub rejects it: "By the time this query traverses to the authors connection, it is requesting
up to 1,000,000 possible nodes which exceeds the maximum limit of 500,000." The cost scales at
~10,000 nodes per PR (limit 60 → 600,000), so any `--limit` above 50 fails. The documented
procedure therefore cannot run as written, and a scan agent following it gets no PR list — every
claimed issue would read as "no PR found".

Evidence: tidy run 2026-09-30T172538-tidy-standalone (reproduced at --limit 200 and --limit 60).

## Deliverables

- Rewrite item 10's third fetch to stay under the node cap — e.g. split by state
  (`open`/`merged`/`closed`, `--limit 45` each) or drop `comments`/`commits` from the bulk list and
  fetch progress per candidate only.
- Match on `refs #N` bodies too, or document that a draft PR with only `refs #N` (as #2822 → #2805)
  is invisible to `closingIssuesReferences` and reads as "no PR found".

## Acceptance Criteria

- Item 10's fetch completes without a GraphQL error on a repo with 200+ PRs.
- A conformance test pins the fetch shape (no `--state all` bulk list carrying both
  `comments` and `commits` above the node budget).

## Release Note

Tidy's unsettled-run check completes on repositories with more than 50 pull requests instead of failing its PR fetch.

Origin: /claude-tweaks:tidy run 2026-09-30T172538-tidy-standalone (approved Step 6 Capture)

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`plugin/bin/lib/issues/claims-git-cas.js:299` (origin/main) calls
`` runner(['cat-file', '--batch'], { input: `${orderedShas.join('\n')}\n`, encoding: 'buffer' }) ``.
With the module's `defaultRunner` (`execFileSync`), Node uses `options.encoding` to encode a
string `input`, and `'buffer'` is not a valid string encoding — Node v22.23.2 throws
`ERR_UNKNOWN_ENCODING` (reproduced: `execFileSync('cat', [], { input: 'x\n', encoding: 'buffer' })`).
The `catch` maps that to `markTransportFailure()`, so every blob returns
`failure: 'transport-failure'` — against this repo's 1293-blob registry, 1293/1293.
`tests/bin-lib/issues/claims-git-cas.test.js` exercises `readClaimBlobsGitBatch` through a fake
runner, so the suite stays green. Downstream effect: tidy Step 4.7's #2613 "never sample" batched
reader is unusable, which pushes scan agents back to sampling — this run's Step 4.7 agent sampled
100 blobs and emitted false release/label-removal rows (every "closed-issue claim" was a
tombstone; every "missed bot:in-progress" issue held a live claim).

Evidence: tidy run 2026-09-30T172538-tidy-standalone, scan/claims-full.jsonl (after a workaround runner).

## Deliverables

- Pass `input` as a Buffer (`Buffer.from(...)`) or drop `encoding: 'buffer'` in favor of reading
  stdout as a Buffer by default, in `readClaimBlobsGitBatch`.
- A test that runs `readClaimBlobsGitBatch` through the real `defaultRunner` against a temp git
  repo with a `claims-registry` tree (not the fake runner).

## Acceptance Criteria

- `readClaimBlobsGitBatch({ tip })` with the default runner returns content (not
  `transport-failure`) for every blob of a real registry tree.
- The new test fails on the current line 299 and passes after the fix.

## Release Note

Tidy's batched claim-registry read works against a real git checkout instead of reporting every claim as a transport failure.

Every local run since the pin fell behind reports these 3 failures, which each pipeline run has to re-diagnose as environmental (the #2827/#2828 run logged them as its ledger item 1). Related: #2531 provisions sandbox plugin caches at whatever the pin is; this record moves the pin itself forward to the version maintainers run, so the two are complementary.

Verified-as-of: c8f389a605ecf680a27528bafef1ef995959fd64

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

`dispatch/SKILL.md` Step 4 mints each group's run dir with `hooks.js resolve-run-dir --spec-slug "record-{n}" --create`. That command still runs resolution-order step 2 (newest directory matching the slug) before minting (`_shared/run-dir-resolution.md`), so it returns an **existing** `record-{n}` directory whenever one is present, including one a live sibling session minted seconds earlier.

Observed in firing `2026-09-29T140150-dispatch-standalone`, group #2785:

- A separate live session (pid 88799) minted `2026-09-29T184002-record-2785` at 18:40:02Z, created worktree `dispatch-record-2785`, and merged `origin/main` into it at 18:40:08Z.
- About two minutes later, this firing's `resolve-run-dir --spec-slug record-2785 --create` returned that sibling-owned directory instead of minting a fresh one. This firing then ran `compose-context.js` against it, rewriting the sibling's `context/claims.md` and `context/merge.md` (identical plugin build and sources, so almost certainly byte-identical, but an unauthorized write into another session's run dir all the same).
- `EnterWorktree(name: "dispatch-record-2785")` then **resumed** the sibling's existing worktree rather than failing. `check-sibling-sessions --record 2785` flagged pid 88799 only when re-run from inside it.

The Step 4 sibling-session check had run earlier (clean, at queue-pull time), not immediately before the mint, so the window between the queue pull and the mint was unguarded. The firing stood down and touched nothing further. On a slower read the two sessions would have built the same record in the same worktree under one run dir.

Related: the "dispatch claim race window: mint to worktree entry" pattern already noted in agent memory. This is the same window, widened to cover the mint itself.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/run-dir-resolve.js`
- `plugin/skills/dispatch/SKILL.md`
- `plugin/skills/dispatch/sibling-session-check.md`
- `plugin/skills/_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md`

## Deliverables

1. A mint-only mode for `resolve-run-dir` (e.g. `--create --fresh`, or `--create` that skips step 2 whenever `--standalone` is absent). It always creates a new timestamped directory and never adopts an existing same-slug one. Use it at dispatch Step 4 and at `flow/claim-targets.md`'s direct-invocation mint. Keep adopt-if-exists behavior for the read-only resolution callers that depend on it.
2. Dispatch Step 4 re-runs `check-sibling-sessions --record {n}` for every group member **immediately before** the mint, not only at queue-pull time. A positive result stops that group, exactly as `sibling-session-check.md` already specifies.
3. Dispatch Step 5 refuses to enter a pre-existing `dispatch-record-{n}` worktree. If the worktree-creation call reports it resumed an existing worktree, the dispatching session exits it with `keep`, logs the sibling conflict, and skips the group without dispatching either call.
4. Tests for (1): a pre-existing same-slug directory is not returned under the mint-only mode; a fresh directory is created and returned.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] With a `record-{n}` run dir already present under `.claude-tweaks/pipelines/`, dispatch Step 4's mint returns a **new** directory, never the existing one.
- [ ] A sibling session holding `record-{n}` (live worktree lock) at mint time stops that group before any write into any run dir.
- [ ] An existing `dispatch-record-{n}` worktree is never resumed by dispatch Step 5; the group is skipped and the skip is logged.
- [ ] Read-only `resolve-run-dir` callers (no `--create`) keep their current adopt-newest-matching behavior.
- [ ] `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

Two sessions dispatching the same record no longer end up sharing one run directory and worktree.

## Current State

`dispatch/two-call-gate.md` section 2 dispatches the second (`review,polish,wrap-up`) call on `DONE`/`DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` **and** `OUTCOME: build-test-ok` alone. `sequential-execution.md` mechanically checks only that the status line is present and well-formed (#2429). Nothing checks that the first call actually ran `/claude-tweaks:flow`, so a self-reported `build-test-ok` from an agent that implemented the record directly passes the gate.

Observed in firing `2026-09-29T140150-dispatch-standalone` (explicit list of 11 records, first calls on the Standard profile with `task-prompt.md`'s first-call template inlined verbatim):

- **#2806, attempt 1** (run dir `2026-09-29T154722-record-2806`): reported `STATUS: DONE` / `OUTCOME: build-test-ok` but never invoked the `/flow` Skill. It implemented the refactor directly, left commit `6fc4e2ded` unpushed, and the run dir held only `context/`: no `decisions.md`, `run-state.json`, `config.yml`, no claim, no `bot:in-progress`, no PR. Its `MANIFEST:` line pointed at `context/claims.md`.
- **#2806, attempt 2** (after resetting the worktree): invoked `Skill claude-tweaks:flow "#2806 build,test"`, then skipped Step 2.8 (claim), the Manifesto (`config.yml`), `run-state.json` and the PR-early push. It implemented directly and materialized the spec *after* the code commit. Again reported `build-test-ok`.
- **#2805**: live claim and draft PR #2822, but no `config.yml`/`run-state.json` (the second call backfilled them).
- **#2792**: full build, but PR-early never ran; the branch stayed unpushed until the second call opened PR #2831.

The dispatching session caught #2806 only by inspecting the run dir by hand. Had #2806 carried `auto:merge`, the second call would have reviewed and possibly merged work that never took a claim or went through PR-early.

This recurs after #1826 (closed 2026-09-23, itself a recurrence of #1013/#1129/#1145), which covered the same "run dir empty despite build commits" symptom. The gate itself was never given an artifact check, so the class remains reachable.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/dispatch/two-call-gate.md`
- `plugin/skills/dispatch/sequential-execution.md`
- `plugin/skills/dispatch/task-prompt.md`
- `plugin/bin/lib/dispatch/artifact-verdict.js`

## Deliverables

1. A mechanical first-call artifact check, run by the dispatching session the moment the first call returns and **before** the two-call gate dispatches the second call. It checks that: `{minted-run-dir}/run-state.json` and `config.yml` exist; the claim blob `claims/issue-{n}.json` on `claims-registry` is live with `runId === basename(PIPELINE_RUN_DIR)` for every group member; and, under `integration-model: pr-first`, `run-state.json` records a `pr.number` whose head branch exists on `origin`. Implement it as a small `bin/` CLI or `bin/lib/dispatch/` function (injectable runner seam per the gh-api-module-pattern), not prose alone.
2. `two-call-gate.md` section 2 and `sequential-execution.md`'s "The loop" treat a failed artifact check exactly like a missing/malformed status line (#2429): never dispatch the second call, route through the section 5 terminal path, and log one `decisions.md` line naming which artifact was missing.
3. Unit tests for the check: a fully-formed run passes; each missing artifact (no `run-state.json`, no `config.yml`, claim absent, claim held under a different `runId`, pr-first with no recorded PR) fails with a distinct reason.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A first call that reports `build-test-ok` but left no claim under the minted run id is never followed by a second-call dispatch, and the firing log names the missing claim.
- [ ] A first call with a live claim but no `config.yml`/`run-state.json` fails the check with a reason naming the missing file.
- [ ] Under `pr-first`, a first call with no recorded PR (or an unpushed head branch) fails the check.
- [ ] A normal, fully-formed first call (claim + `run-state.json` + `config.yml` + pushed PR) passes and the second call dispatches unchanged.
- [ ] `two-call-gate.md` section 2 states the artifact check as a gate condition alongside STATUS/OUTCOME, and cites the check's module.
- [ ] `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

Dispatch no longer proceeds to review and merge when a build agent reports success without actually running the pipeline.

Surface: infra

## Current State

A named "Advisor Pattern" (a cheap/fast model executes, a stronger model advises/reviews) is reported externally to beat a mid-tier model alone at lower cost. claude-tweaks currently has no documented practice of this shape — model selection today is either a single model for the whole task, or the existing Subagent Contract's static Fast/Standard/Capable profile per dispatch, not a two-model advise/execute split within one task.

## Deliverables

Evaluate the Advisor Pattern against one representative claude-tweaks task (a build, a review, or a similarly-scoped unit of work) by running it once under the pattern (a fast/cheap model executing, a stronger model reviewing/advising) and once under the current default approach for the same task, then compare cost and output quality between the two runs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One sample task is run both ways (Advisor Pattern vs. current default), with actual token/cost figures and a quality comparison (not just cost) reported for both.
- A recommendation is recorded: adopt the pattern for some class of claude-tweaks work (naming which), or don't, with the comparison data as the stated justification either way.
- If adopted, the recommendation states specifically which of claude-tweaks' own workflows (build, review, dispatch, etc.) it would apply to — not a blanket claim it should replace all current model selection.

## Release Note

No user-visible change: measured whether pairing a fast executing model with a stronger advising model improves cost and quality.

## Technical Approach

Pick one bounded, representative task (small enough to run twice affordably, substantial enough that quality differences would actually show) and execute it under both configurations, capturing real cost and quality data from each run rather than estimating. Compare against the Subagent Contract's existing static Fast/Standard/Capable guidance to determine whether the Advisor Pattern is complementary (a specific dispatch shape within that existing framework) or a genuinely separate mechanism.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — the existing model-selection guidance to compare the pattern against

## Gotchas

- A single sample task's comparison is a screening signal, not a proof — state the recommendation's confidence level accordingly rather than over-generalizing from one data point.
- Cost and quality can trade off in either direction depending on task shape — don't assume the externally-reported result (Advisor Pattern beats mid-tier alone) transfers unchanged to claude-tweaks' own task shapes without actually measuring it here, which is exactly what this record's Deliverable requires.

## Original request

Evaluate the Haiku+Opus "Advisor Pattern" for cost/quality

Context: A named 'Advisor Pattern' (cheap model executes, stronger model advises/reviews) reportedly beats a mid-tier model alone at lower cost.

Scope: Evaluate the pattern against a sample claude-tweaks task and compare cost/quality to the current default.

Surface: infra

## Current State

`jev-model-router` picks model and reasoning effort per Claude Code turn via a non-blocking hook. claude-tweaks today has model-profile selection guidance for subagent dispatch (Fast/Standard/Capable, per the Subagent Contract referenced in CLAUDE.md's Model Selection section), but no automatic per-turn picker for the *main* session's own model/effort choice — that decision is currently manual (`/fast` toggle, explicit model selection). Whether an automatic per-turn picker would meaningfully improve on the current manual/subagent-scoped approach, versus adding complexity for marginal gain, has not been evaluated.

## Deliverables

Investigate `jev-model-router`'s actual mechanism (what signals it uses to pick model/effort, how it hooks into the turn lifecycle) and decide whether a similar fast decision-layer fits claude-tweaks' build/flow lifecycle specifically — not the main interactive session broadly, since that's Claude Code's own territory, not this plugin's. Scope the evaluation to where claude-tweaks itself dispatches subagents (build/flow/dispatch's Task and Agent calls) and whether an automatic picker there would improve on the Subagent Contract's existing static Fast/Standard/Capable model-profile guidance.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `jev-model-router`'s actual selection mechanism is investigated and summarized (what it reads, how it decides, where it hooks in) — not assumed from the capture's one-line description.
- A decision is recorded: either a concrete proposal for how per-turn/per-dispatch picking would integrate with the existing Subagent Contract's model-profile guidance (with a clear delta over the current static guidance), or a documented reason the static approach is preferred and why, so the question isn't silently re-raised later without the comparison already on record.
- If a picker is proposed, it is scoped to claude-tweaks' own dispatch call sites (build/flow/dispatch), not the main interactive session, which is Claude Code's own territory.

## Release Note

No user-visible change: evaluated a per-turn model and effort picker for the build lifecycle.

## Technical Approach

Research `jev-model-router`'s public documentation/source for its actual decision mechanism first. Compare against the Subagent Contract's existing Model Selection section (referenced from root CLAUDE.md) — what signals a dispatcher currently uses to pick Fast/Standard/Capable, and whether an automatic picker would improve on that or just add indirection. This is investigation-first: the record intentionally doesn't presuppose that adopting a router-style mechanism is the right outcome.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — the existing static Model Selection guidance this evaluation compares against

## Gotchas

- Scope this to claude-tweaks' own subagent dispatch sites specifically — an automatic picker for the *main* interactive session's own model choice is Claude Code platform territory, not something this plugin can or should implement.
- Don't adopt "automatic" as inherently better than "documented static guidance a human/dispatcher reads" without a concrete case for what the automation actually improves — added complexity needs to earn its keep over the current approach.

## Original request

Consider a jev-model-router-style per-turn model/effort picker

Context: jev-model-router picks model and reasoning effort per Claude Code turn via a non-blocking hook.

Scope: Whether a similar fast decision-layer per-turn picker fits claude-tweaks' build/flow lifecycle.

Surface: infra

## Current State

No canonical bounded-polling idiom exists for a subagent that must wait on a genuinely long external process (e.g. a live CI run or cloud deploy taking many minutes) without violating the "never run_in_background, never end a turn on a passive wait" rule.

A subagent's own work required verifying a live external process spanning many minutes (a CI run, a cloud deployment dispatch) across several such waits in one session. The rule correctly forbids backgrounding plus a passive wait (a background task's completion notification never reaches an orchestrator watching a dispatched agent) but offers no first-class alternative pattern for this shape of task. The only compliant approach found was a hand-rolled bounded polling loop repeated across several tool calls (a shell `while` loop checking a condition every ~15s, bounded to a fixed iteration count, re-invoked when the loop exhausted its bound without the condition resolving).

This worked, but:
- It's easy to get subtly wrong — the natural first instinct is backgrounding plus a wait, exactly the forbidden pattern.
- From outside, "an agent doing bounded polling with real tool calls" and "an agent stuck in a silent loop" are hard to distinguish without inspecting the transcript. A coordinating session watching the dispatched work sent live check-in interruptions during a genuinely-compliant polling sequence, which turned out to be false alarms once investigated.

## Deliverables

Document a canonical bounded-polling idiom for "wait on a genuinely long external process without backgrounding": the exact loop shape, the iteration/timeout budget, and what to log so an external observer can tell "polling as designed" apart from "stuck."

## Acceptance Criteria

- The canonical idiom is documented in the dispatch/subagent-contract shared guidance (the exact home to be confirmed against this repo's current shared-contract layout — `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` is the most likely fit, since it already owns the dispatch-behavior conventions this gap sits alongside).
- The documented idiom specifies: the loop shape (a bounded check-interval loop, not backgrounding), a concrete iteration/timeout budget (not left open-ended), and a logging convention that lets an external observer distinguish "polling as designed, still within budget" from "appears stuck."
- A subagent following the documented idiom for a multi-minute external wait no longer needs to hand-roll the pattern from scratch, and a coordinating session reading its progress has a documented signal to check before interrupting.

## Release Note

Documented a standard way for subagents to wait on long external processes without looking stuck.

## Technical Approach

Locate the existing "never run_in_background, never end a turn on a passive wait" rule's canonical home in this repo's shared skill guidance (search `plugin/skills/_shared/` and `docs/skill-authoring.md` for where dispatch/subagent behavioral rules already live) before adding the new idiom — it should sit alongside that rule, not in a new, disconnected location. Compose the idiom from the pattern already proven to work in practice: a bounded check-interval loop (real tool calls, not a background process) with a fixed iteration cap, re-entered when the cap is exhausted without resolution, plus a per-iteration log line naming what's being waited on and the current iteration count — that log line is what lets an external observer tell "polling as designed" apart from "stuck."

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — most likely home for the new idiom, alongside existing dispatch-behavior conventions (confirm before writing; the exact section may differ)
- `docs/skill-authoring.md` — cross-check for whether dispatch/polling conventions are documented there instead

## Gotchas

- Confirm the actual canonical location of the existing no-background-wait rule before adding the new idiom next to it — this record's own research did not pin the exact file, only the most likely candidate.
- The logging convention (Acceptance Criteria) matters as much as the loop shape itself — the real-world cost this record documents (false-alarm interruptions from a coordinating session) came specifically from the *absence* of a way to externally distinguish compliant polling from a stuck loop, not from the polling mechanism itself being wrong.

## Original request

**Summary:** No canonical bounded-polling idiom for a subagent that must wait on a genuinely long external process (e.g. a live CI run or cloud deploy taking many minutes) without violating the "never run_in_background, never end a turn on a passive wait" rule.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** Subagent Contract / dispatch guidance (the no-background-wait rule and its documentation)

**Use case:** A subagent's own work required verifying a live external process spanning many minutes (a CI run, a cloud deployment dispatch) across several such waits in one session. The Subagent Contract correctly forbids `run_in_background` plus a passive wait (a background task's completion notification never reaches an orchestrator watching a dispatched agent) but offers no first-class alternative pattern for this shape of task. The only compliant approach found was a hand-rolled bounded polling loop repeated across several tool calls (a shell `while` loop checking a condition every ~15s, bounded to a fixed iteration count, re-invoked when the loop exhausted its bound without the condition resolving).

This worked, but:
- It's easy to get subtly wrong — the natural first instinct is `run_in_background` + wait, exactly the forbidden pattern.
- From outside, "an agent doing bounded polling with real tool calls" and "an agent stuck in a silent loop" are hard to distinguish without inspecting the transcript. A coordinating session watching the dispatched work sent live check-in interruptions during a genuinely-compliant polling sequence, which turned out to be false alarms once investigated.

**Suggested resolution:** Document a canonical bounded-polling idiom (e.g. in the dispatch-core shared guidance) for "wait on a genuinely long external process without backgrounding" — the exact loop shape, the iteration/timeout budget, and what to log so an external observer can tell "polling as designed" apart from "stuck."

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.129.0

Surface: infra

## Current State

When `/claude-tweaks:specify` shapes a record whose Deliverables prescribe the algorithm of a security-shaped check keyed on a path, URI, hostname or identity string, its red-team (`plugin/skills/specify/red-team.md`) only probes the substring-spoof case; the resulting spec's test list is what every later review compares the code against, so dot-segment and mount-prefix bypasses reach the last review lens before anything probes them.

**Real incident this record generalizes from:** a record shaped by `/claude-tweaks:specify` prescribed a guard — "allow the feature only when the storage root is a sandbox root — the URI path contains a `sandbox` segment; otherwise refuse" — together with its test list. The red-team probed "the word `sandbox` inside the storage-account name" and nothing else. The build's task review and the whole-branch review both validated the implementation against that text (12 root shapes probed, none containing a dot segment) and passed it. Only the Security lens of `/claude-tweaks:review`, the last gate, found that `<scheme>://<account>/sandbox/../artifacts` passed the guard while the storage layer normalizes it to the production-equivalent root, and that a mounted-storage prefix was treated as a local path.

Why it is systemic (reflect's near-miss chain walk, causal: systemic):
1. The spec prescribed the guard's algorithm and its test cases; every later reviewer compared the code to that text.
2. The plan carried the spec's test list verbatim, so no adversarial case existed to fail.
3. The first two review layers compare code to spec; only the lens pass probes inputs — so a security-shaped check receives adversarial input for the first time at the last gate.

Cost: one extra fix dispatch plus one full re-verification run (about eight minutes) after two reviews had already approved the guard; at a `low` review tier the lens would not have run and the bypass would have shipped.

## Deliverables

Extend `/claude-tweaks:specify`'s red-team (`red-team.md`) so that, when an Acceptance Criterion or Deliverable prescribes a decision keyed on a path, URI, hostname, or identity string, the red-team requires the AC to enumerate adversarial inputs before the spec is marked shaped: dot segments (`.`/`..`) before and after normalization, mount/scheme variants, uppercase schemes, percent-encoding, trailing slashes, and the "substring in the wrong component" case it already covers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `red-team.md` documents the new detection trigger (an AC/Deliverable prescribing a path/URI/hostname/identity-keyed decision) and the adversarial-input checklist it now requires (dot segments pre/post normalization, mount/scheme variants, uppercase schemes, percent-encoding, trailing slashes, substring-in-wrong-component).
- Re-shaping a record matching the incident's own guard shape (a path/URI containment check) via `/claude-tweaks:specify` produces an Acceptance Criteria section enumerating the new adversarial cases, not just the substring-spoof case it already covered.
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s Security lens (`3b`) and the new red-team checklist are checked for consistency — pulling from the same probe list, per the filed suggestion, so the shaping gate and the last review lens probe the same adversarial set rather than diverging.

## Release Note

Made the spec red-team demand adversarial inputs whenever a spec guards on a path, URL, or identity.

## Technical Approach

Add a detection step to `red-team.md`'s existing procedure: scan the composed Acceptance Criteria/Deliverables text for path/URI/hostname/identity-guard language (containment checks, prefix/segment matching, "must be under X root" phrasing) — the same class of language the incident's own guard used. When detected, require the AC to name the adversarial-input checklist above before the spec can be marked shaped, mirroring how the existing substring-spoof case is already required. Cross-reference `step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s Security lens (3b) to pull from the same checklist where practical, so the two checks stay in sync rather than drifting into two separately-maintained adversarial-input lists.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/specify/red-team.md` — the red-team procedure to extend with the new detection trigger and checklist
- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` — Security lens (3b), to cross-reference for probe-list consistency

## Gotchas

- The detection trigger (path/URI/hostname/identity-guard language) needs to be specific enough to fire on the real pattern (containment/prefix/segment checks) without false-triggering on every record that merely mentions a file path — over-triggering would add checklist ceremony to unrelated records and train users to ignore it (the same anti-pattern `challenge/SKILL.md`'s framing-check explicitly warns against for its own signal).
- The adversarial-input checklist (dot segments, mount/scheme variants, percent-encoding, etc.) should stay a single source of truth shared between this red-team check and the review Security lens, not two independently-maintained copies that drift apart over time — Acceptance Criteria 3 above exists specifically to catch that drift at build time, not just at this record's own merge.

## Original request

**Summary:** When `/claude-tweaks:specify` shapes a record whose Deliverables prescribe the algorithm of a security-shaped check keyed on a path, URI, hostname or identity string, its red-team only probes the substring-spoof case; the resulting spec's test list is what every later review compares the code against, so dot-segment and mount-prefix bypasses reach the last review lens before anything probes them.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** `/claude-tweaks:specify` (the shaping red-team over Acceptance Criteria); interacts with `/claude-tweaks:build`'s task review and `/claude-tweaks:review`'s Security lens

**Use case:** In a private project, a record shaped by `/claude-tweaks:specify` prescribed a guard: "allow the feature only when the storage root is a sandbox root — the URI path contains a `sandbox` segment; otherwise refuse", together with its test list. The red-team probed "the word `sandbox` inside the storage-account name" and nothing else. The build's task review and the whole-branch review both validated the implementation against that text (12 root shapes probed, none containing a dot segment) and passed it. Only the Security lens of `/claude-tweaks:review`, the last gate, found that `<scheme>://<account>/sandbox/../artifacts` passed the guard while the storage layer normalizes it to the production-equivalent root, and that a mounted-storage prefix was treated as a local path.

Why it is systemic (reflect's near-miss chain walk, causal: systemic):
1. The spec prescribed the guard's algorithm and its test cases; every later reviewer compared the code to that text.
2. The plan carried the spec's test list verbatim, so no adversarial case existed to fail.
3. The first two review layers compare code to spec; only the lens pass probes inputs — so a security-shaped check receives adversarial input for the first time at the last gate.

Cost: one extra fix dispatch plus one full re-verification run (about eight minutes) after two reviews had already approved the guard; at a `low` review tier the lens would not have run and the bypass would have shipped.

Suggested change: in `/claude-tweaks:specify`'s red-team, when an Acceptance Criterion or Deliverable prescribes a decision keyed on a path, URI, hostname or identity string, require the AC to enumerate adversarial inputs before the spec is marked shaped: dot segments (`.`/`..`) before and after normalization, mount/scheme variants, uppercase schemes, percent-encoding, trailing slashes, and the "substring in the wrong component" case it already covers. Lifting them from the same probe list the review's Security lens uses would make the shaping gate and the last lens probe the same set.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.129.0

Defer-reason: tangential

## Current State

During #2697's Common Step 5 full verification (runner `verify.js`, tree `d5343fdf7`, 9360 tests /
9012 pass / 343 fail), `tests/bin-lib/log-decision/append.test.js` failed once — the **only** failing
file not in the run's batch pre-flight baseline (run ledger #2, 103 files).

Failing test: ``appendEntry: concurrent `node bin/log-decision.js` processes against the same run dir
never drop an entry``. Failure: `worker 2 exited 3: could not write decisions.md (EPERM: operation not
permitted, rename '…decisions.md.tmp-26780' -> '…decisions.md')` — a Windows atomic-rename collision
between concurrent writers under machine load.

Nothing on the branch touched `plugin/bin/lib/log-decision/`. Isolated re-run
`node --test tests/bin-lib/log-decision/append.test.js`: 9/9 pass. So the failure is load-dependent,
not a regression.

## Deliverables

Pick one of two mutually exclusive routes and state why the other was not chosen:

1. **Allowlist the test.** Add `tests/bin-lib/log-decision/append.test.js` to
   `.claude-tweaks/verify-scope.json`'s `flaky.files`. If the declaration carries no `retry` template
   for the `tests` suite yet, add it alongside: `"retry": "node --test {file}"` and
   `"maxRetries": 1`. Without **both**, the entry is incomplete (`test/verification.md`'s Flake
   handling).
2. **Fix the product behavior the test guards.** The test asserts a real concurrency property, and on
   Windows `fs.rename` over an open target returns `EPERM`. A bounded, Windows-only retry loop in
   `plugin/bin/lib/atomic-write.js`'s rename would make the guarded behavior actually hold rather than
   declaring its test flaky. This is the better outcome if the retry is cheap to bound correctly —
   `log-decision.js` is a sanctioned run-dir writer that concurrent sibling agents genuinely hammer.

## Acceptance Criteria

Route 1: a `verify.js` run whose `tests/bin-lib/log-decision/append.test.js` fails once retries it and
reports the file as passing; the `flaky.files` entry carries both `retry` and `maxRetries`.

Route 2: the concurrent-writers test passes under deliberate contention on this Windows box (run it
with sibling load, quote the raw output), with no allowlist entry added; `atomic-write.js`'s retry is
bounded and covered by its own regression test.

## Release Note

Stopped a decision-log test from failing intermittently on Windows under load.

## Technical Approach

Start with Route 2's feasibility check: read `plugin/bin/lib/atomic-write.js`'s current rename call. If it already has any retry scaffolding, a bounded Windows-only `EPERM` retry (a handful of attempts with a short backoff, gated to `process.platform === 'win32'`) is likely a small, contained addition. If the rename is a bare single-shot call with no surrounding structure, Route 1 (allowlist) is the cheaper, lower-risk choice — `.claude-tweaks/verify-scope.json`'s `flaky.files` shape is documented in `test/verification.md`'s Flake handling section. Whichever route is chosen, the record's own AC requires stating why the other was declined — this is not optional per the Deliverables text.

### Key Files

- `.claude-tweaks/verify-scope.json` — Route 1's allowlist entry (`flaky.files`, `retry`, `maxRetries`)
- `plugin/bin/lib/atomic-write.js` — Route 2's bounded rename retry
- `tests/bin-lib/log-decision/append.test.js` — the guarded concurrency property; Route 2 adds a regression test near this one if the fix lands here instead
- `plugin/bin/log-decision.js` — the sanctioned run-dir writer this test guards

## Gotchas

- The two routes are mutually exclusive by design — don't do both. Route 1 accepts the flake as an environmental Windows limitation; Route 2 asserts the underlying behavior should actually hold. Pick based on how cheap a *correctly bounded* retry actually is once `atomic-write.js`'s current rename call is read — don't assume either route without that read first.

Surface: infra

## Current State

`plugin/skills/_shared/criteria-security-hardening.md` and its generator, `plugin/bin/lib/code-health/candidates-security-hardening.js`, currently detect exactly three candidate kinds — `client-secret`, `missing-ownership-check`, `unguarded-ai-endpoint` (that file's own "Scope boundary" section names the vertical's exact three-check ownership, #2624). None of the three check for agent/tool identity separation, scoped-vs-broad tool permissions, or credential lifetime — the class of risk the filed source (an article framing prompt injection as an authorization failure, not a detection problem) argues for: assume injection succeeds, and limit what a compromised agent call can actually reach. claude-tweaks' own subagent dispatch (`plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`) has no documented per-agent identity or credential-scoping check today.

## Deliverables

- A fourth candidate kind for the security-hardening generator (`candidates-security-hardening.js`) and a matching criteria section in `criteria-security-hardening.md`, following that file's existing per-check format (What to flag / What NOT to flag / a copy-paste prompt), covering: agents/tools sharing one broad-access identity or token instead of distinct, scoped identities; and delegation chains (one agent calling another, or a tool call) with no audit-log/trace of who delegated to whom.
- A one-time, hand-run application of the new check against claude-tweaks' own dispatch model (`_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`, `bin/hooks.js`'s dispatch-adjacent code) reported as a pass/fail per mitigation in this record's own PR description or a follow-up comment — this is a self-audit exercise, not a generator capability, since the generator's own scope (per its file header) is scanning *other* AI-built apps' source, not this plugin's own architecture.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `criteria-security-hardening.md` documents the new candidate kind in the same structural shape as the existing three (What to flag / What NOT to flag / one copy-paste prompt), and `candidates-security-hardening.js` emits it for a recognizable pattern (a shared/hardcoded credential or token reused across multiple call sites with no per-caller scoping, or a delegation call with no accompanying log/trace statement).
- Running `/claude-tweaks:code-health --focus=security-hardening` (or the equivalent focus-mode invocation) against a fixture containing the new pattern produces at least one finding of the new kind.
- The dispatch self-audit (Deliverable 2) is written up as a pass/fail per mitigation (identity separation, scoped permissions, credential lifetime, delegation audit) against claude-tweaks' actual subagent contract — not asserted without the write-up.

## Release Note

Added security checks for per-agent identity and narrowly scoped credentials.

## Technical Approach

Extend `candidates-security-hardening.js` with a fourth `kind` following the same generator shape the existing three use (a `{ file, kind, evidence }` candidate, a text-pattern detector, not a semantic/AST analysis — per the file's own "starting pointer, not a finding" framing). Detection signal: a credential/token variable name or literal reused verbatim across two or more distinct call sites that look like separate callers/agents (heuristic, approximate — the criteria doc's own "What NOT to flag" convention applies: false positives get filtered at judgment time, not generation time). Add the matching `## What to flag` / `## What NOT to flag` / copy-paste-prompt entries to `criteria-security-hardening.md`, keyed to this new kind, mirroring the three existing entries' structure exactly. The self-audit deliverable is separate from the generator change — it's a one-time manual application of the new criteria against this repo's own dispatch contract, reported in prose, not a new automated check running against claude-tweaks itself (the generator's stated scope is external AI-built apps, per its own header — extending it to self-scan is out of scope for this record).

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/code-health/candidates-security-hardening.js` — add the fourth candidate kind's detection logic
- `plugin/skills/_shared/criteria-security-hardening.md` — add the matching criteria section (What to flag / What NOT to flag / copy-paste prompt)
- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — read (not edited) as the audit target for the self-audit deliverable

**Related:** #2749 (autonomous-agent blast-radius hardening check — same security-hardening vertical, adjacent but distinct mitigation: blast-radius/scope limiting vs. this record's identity/credential-lifetime focus)

## Gotchas

- The record's two Acceptance Criteria pull in different directions: AC 1 (a generator check for *any* scanned codebase) is the vertical's normal shape; AC 2 (apply it to dispatch's own credential model) is a one-time self-audit, not a capability the generator itself gains. Treat them as two separate deliverables, not one mechanism doing both — conflating them risks either under-scoping the generator change or over-scoping it into a self-monitoring feature nobody asked for.
- Detecting "shared identity" or "delegation with no audit log" from static text alone is inherently heuristic — the existing three checks already accept this tradeoff (`missing-ownership-check` and `unguarded-ai-endpoint`'s own "What NOT to flag" sections exist for exactly this reason); expect meaningful false-positive tuning after the first real-world run, not a one-shot precise detector.
- claude-tweaks' own subagent dispatch may turn out to already satisfy some mitigations informally (e.g. `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` scoping) — the self-audit should report what's actually true, not assume every mitigation is missing just because no formal check existed before this record.

## Original request

Add per-agent identity and scoped-credential hardening checks

Current State:
- Argues prompt injection is fundamentally an authorization failure: assume injection succeeds and limit what a compromised agent call can reach, rather than only trying to detect bad input.
- Proposes four concrete mitigations: distinct identity per agent, per-tool scoped permissions, short-lived on-demand credentials, and audit logs of delegation chains.
- claude-tweaks' current hardening guidance doesn't yet check for per-agent identity separation or credential lifetime.
Deliverables:
- A hardening checklist item (in /security-review or a new lens) verifying agents/tools use distinct identities, scoped permissions, and short-lived credentials rather than shared broad-access tokens.
- A delegation-chain audit-log requirement for any skill that lets one agent call another.
Acceptance Criteria:
- The checklist runs as part of /security-review.
- Applying it to dispatch's own agent-to-tool credential model reports pass/fail per mitigation.
Source: https://medium.com/@paoloperrone/prompt-injection-is-an-authorization-bug-56657b62783f

Surface: infra

## Current State

`/claude-tweaks:review`'s lens system (`plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md`, `### 3a`-`### 3f`) currently dispatches six lenses — Convention Compliance, Security, Error Handling, Performance, Architecture, Test Quality — none of which asks whether a human on-call owner would understand and accept responsibility for the code under review. `/claude-tweaks:code-health`'s own checklist (`plugin/skills/code-health/SKILL.md`) is similarly scoped to correctness/debt classes, not comprehension risk. As a result, code that passes every existing lens — tests green, conventions followed, no security/perf/architecture flags — can still be the kind of output a teammate would hesitate to own: dense, unexplained, or relying on implicit context no PR description states. The filed source (a senior engineer's account of deleting 3,000 lines of working, tested AI-generated code because the team couldn't explain it) is an anecdote illustrating the gap, not a technology choice to justify.

## Deliverables

- A new lens, `### 3g: Ownability`, added to `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md`'s Lens definitions section (3a-3f), following the existing lenses' own format (scope, what it flags, output shape).
- A short rubric embedded in that lens definition: the concrete question a reviewer (human or agent) applies — could an on-call engineer debug this at 3am without the PR description open? — expressed as checkable signals (unexplained non-obvious control flow, a mechanism with no comment or spec context explaining *why*, a diff whose Deliverables/AC don't mention why this shape was chosen), not a vague restatement of the question itself.
- The new lens wired into `code-mode-steps.md`'s Step 3 lens dispatch/debate/routing exactly as 3a-3f already are, so it participates in the same fan-out, debate, and Step 3 Routing consolidation as the existing six.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` documents lens `3g: Ownability` in the same structural shape as `3a`-`3f` (a scope line, concrete flag signals, and an output/finding shape consistent with the other lenses).
- `code-mode-steps.md`'s Step 3 lens list includes 3g alongside 3a-3f (dispatch, debate-and-refutation, and Step 3 Routing all iterate the full lens set, not a hardcoded 3a-3f range).
- Running the new lens against a sample diff that is dense/unexplained but otherwise clean (passes tests, follows conventions, no security/perf/architecture issues) produces at least one ownability finding — verified by hand-testing the lens against one such diff before merge.
- The rubric is stated as concrete signals a reviewer checks, not as an open-ended restatement of "would someone understand this."

## Release Note

Added a review lens that checks whether new code is easy for the team to own and maintain.

## Technical Approach

Add lens 3g following the existing 3a-3f pattern in `step3-lens-dispatch.md`: a scope description (what content class the lens reads — the diff plus the record's Deliverables/Technical Approach for stated rationale), the flag signals (control flow with no explaining comment or spec cross-reference; a diff whose composed record gives no reason for the specific mechanism chosen; dense multi-concern functions with no narrative), and the finding output shape matching 3a-3f's existing convention. Update `code-mode-steps.md`'s Step 3 lens enumeration and `step3-debate-and-refutation.md`/`step3-routing.md` wherever they name the lens set explicitly (both files iterate lenses generically per a quick read of their current content, so this may be a no-op beyond the two files above — confirm before assuming a third edit site).

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/review/step3-lens-dispatch.md` — add `### 3g: Ownability` to the Lens definitions section (after 3f)
- `plugin/skills/review/code-mode-steps.md` — extend Step 3's lens fan-out to include 3g

## Gotchas

- The rubric must resolve to concrete, checkable signals — a lens whose only instruction is "would a teammate understand this?" produces inconsistent findings across runs. Anchor it the way 3a-3f anchor their own scope (specific content patterns to flag), not a restated question.
- This lens necessarily overlaps in spirit with Architecture (3e) and Convention Compliance (3a) — scope it narrowly to *comprehension/ownership* risk (would a maintainer accept responsibility for this) rather than duplicating those lenses' existing structural/convention checks, or Step 3 Routing's consolidation will just collapse near-duplicate findings.
- "Flags at least one comprehension risk when present" (AC 3) needs a concrete sample diff to hand-test against before merge — pick or construct one that is deliberately dense/unexplained-but-clean so the AC is actually falsifiable, not asserted.

## Original request

Add an ownability/maintainability check to the review lens

Current State:
- A senior engineer deleted 3,000 lines of AI-generated code that passed tests and worked, because the team couldn't explain it and didn't want to be paged for it.
- claude-tweaks' /review and /code-review currently judge correctness, reuse, simplification, and efficiency, but nothing explicitly checks whether an on-call owner would understand and accept responsibility for the code.
Deliverables:
- A maintainability/ownability check added to /review (or /code-health) that flags code a teammate would hesitate to own, even when tests pass.
- A short rubric: could someone debug this at 3am without the PR description?
Acceptance Criteria:
- The check is documented as a policy row usable by /code-health or /review.
- Running it against a sample AI-generated diff flags at least one comprehension risk when present.
Source: https://medium.com/@webdeveloper45/my-senior-engineer-deleted-3-000-lines-of-ai-generated-code-on-friday-6f1869c91f3d

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

Task reviewers dispatched by `/claude-tweaks:build`'s subagent-driven-development (SDD) loop (`plugin/skills/build/dispatch.md` and related SDD prompt composition) are told they are read-only but not how to run a discrimination check safely, and none of the SDD templates demand the Subagent Contract's first-line status token — so one reviewer reverted a file in the shared worktree, and every SDD subagent reply this run was logged as a `contract-violation`.

A multi-spec `/flow` run in one shared worktree: a task reviewer wanted to prove a new test discriminates, so it ran `git checkout -- <source file>` in place, watched the test fail, and restored the file — the tree ended up clean, but a concurrent implementer on the same worktree would have lost its edit, and the controller only noticed by reading the report. Separately, the run's `friction-events.js` output listed 15 `contract-violation` events, all of them SDD subagents whose first line was a markdown heading ("### Spec Compliance", "## Strengths", "### Finding Verdicts") or an in-body "Status: DONE" — the templates never ask for the DONE/DONE_WITH_CONCERNS/NEEDS_CONTEXT/BLOCKED first line (the Subagent Contract's own required status line, `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`), so the detector fires on every one and the Friction lens has to discount them by hand.

## Deliverables

- Every reviewer dispatch composed by `/build`'s SDD loop states explicitly: "never mutate the working tree — a discrimination check that needs a reverted or edited file runs in a scratch `git worktree add`, never in place." This is a prompt-text addition to the reviewer/re-review dispatch composition, not a mechanical enforcement (SDD reviewers run in a shared worktree by design, so this is a stated rule the agent must follow, the same way other read-only dispatch constraints in this codebase are prompt-stated rather than sandboxed).
- Prepend the Subagent Contract's first-line status-token requirement (`DONE`/`DONE_WITH_CONCERNS`/`NEEDS_CONTEXT`/`BLOCKED`) to the SDD implementer/reviewer/re-review templates, so their replies satisfy the same contract every other dispatched subagent in this codebase already follows.
- Confirm the `friction-events.js` `contract-violation` detector recognizes the corrected SDD templates' status line correctly after the template change (it should stop over-firing once the templates comply, with no detector change needed — verify this rather than assuming it).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The SDD implementer, task-reviewer, and re-review prompt templates in `/build`'s dispatch composition each open with the required status-token line and state the tree-immutability rule (scratch worktree for any discrimination check that needs to revert/mutate a file).
- A fresh SDD dispatch run produces zero `contract-violation` events attributable to a missing/malformed status line on an SDD subagent reply.
- `npm test` passes.

## Release Note

Made review subagents leave the working tree untouched and open their reply with a status line.

## Technical Approach

Locate every SDD dispatch prompt composition site in `plugin/skills/build/dispatch.md` (and any sibling file it delegates to for implementer/reviewer/re-review prompt text) and add both requirements inline in the composed prompt block itself — per `docs/skill-authoring.md`'s "Everything the agent must satisfy goes inside the inlined block" rule, a requirement stated only in the surrounding skill prose never reaches the dispatched agent. Cross-reference `_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` for the canonical status-token wording rather than inventing new phrasing.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/build/dispatch.md` — the SDD dispatch composition site(s) needing both additions
- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — canonical status-token wording to reuse verbatim
- `plugin/bin/friction-events.js` (or wherever the `contract-violation` detector lives) — verify, don't just assume, that it correctly recognizes the corrected templates' status line post-fix

## Gotchas

- The tree-immutability rule is prompt-stated, not mechanically enforced — a reviewer that ignores the instruction can still mutate the shared worktree; this record's fix reduces the chance of a repeat, it doesn't eliminate the underlying shared-worktree risk architecturally.
- Don't assume the `contract-violation` detector itself is broken — the 15 false positives this session came from the templates never emitting the required first line at all, not from the detector misreading a compliant line. Verify the detector's behavior against a corrected template rather than also rewriting detector logic that may already be correct.

## Original request

build: SDD reviewer dispatches lack a tree-immutability rule and the first-line status token

**Summary:** Task reviewers dispatched by `/claude-tweaks:build`'s subagent-driven-development loop are told they are read-only but not how to run a discrimination check safely, and none of the SDD templates demand the Subagent Contract's first-line status token — so one reviewer reverted a file in the shared worktree, and every SDD subagent reply this run was logged as a `contract-violation`.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** `/claude-tweaks:build` SDD dispatch composition (implementer / task-reviewer / re-review prompts) and the SubagentStop `contract-violation` detector

**Use case:** A multi-spec `/flow` run in one shared worktree. A task reviewer wanted to prove a new test discriminates, so it ran `git checkout -- <source file>` in place, watched the test fail, and restored the file — the tree ended up clean, but a concurrent implementer on the same worktree would have lost its edit, and the controller only noticed by reading the report. Separately, the run's `friction-events.js` output listed 15 `contract-violation` events, all of them SDD subagents whose first line was a markdown heading ("### Spec Compliance", "## Strengths", "### Finding Verdicts") or an in-body "Status: DONE" — the templates never ask for the DONE/DONE_WITH_CONCERNS/NEEDS_CONTEXT/BLOCKED first line, so the detector fires on every one and the Friction lens has to discount them by hand.

Suggested: (1) every reviewer dispatch composed by `/build` states "never mutate the working tree — a discrimination check that needs a reverted or edited file runs in a scratch `git worktree add`, never in place"; (2) prepend the first-line status-token requirement to the SDD implementer/reviewer/re-review templates (or teach the detector those templates' own status line) so `contract-violation` stops over-reporting on them.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.126.0

Surface: backend

## Current State

`refine-closing-summary.md` documents that the closing tally line is derived by "counting these lines by type" from the run's own `decisions.md` log. In a session on 2026-09-20, a whole-queue `/claude-tweaks:backlog refine` run's rendered closing summary stated "40 priority set (19 this run + this batch) · 3 Related updated · ... · 3 collision-reconciled · 0 failed" — but the run's own `decisions.md` contains exactly 19 `refine #N` priority-set entries, and the surrounding table in the same message lists exactly 19 records. The "40" figure conflated the count of labels resolved by this run's writes with the size of a different, 40-record population (the grant-check candidates, none of which this run actually wrote a priority label to — those already carried one from a concurrent actor). `collision-reconciled` is also not one of `refine-closing-summary.md`'s enumerated tally fields — confirmed absent from the current skill prose (`grep -rn "collision-reconciled" plugin/` returns no hits). Separately, a later closing message for that same skill stated "writing the watermark" as an action about to be taken, when the only subsequent action was deleting scratch files — the session-evaluation self-assessment path never writes a watermark by design, so the claim was never going to be backed by an actual write.

## Deliverables

- Add a small mechanical helper (a `hooks.js` subcommand, or extend `bin/log-decision.js`'s sibling tooling) that derives a refine run's closing tally directly from its own `decisions.md` entries by type, so the rendered summary cannot state a count its own audit trail doesn't support.
- Constrain the closing summary's tally vocabulary to `refine-closing-summary.md`'s enumerated fields only (or document `collision-reconciled` there if it's a legitimate addition worth keeping).
- Where a skill step is about to state a specific action in its closing text ("writing the watermark," "closing the run"), require that the action actually execute (or the claim be omitted) before that sentence renders — particularly relevant for the self-assessment degradation path, which by design skips several actions a dispatched-judge path would take.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A `/claude-tweaks:backlog refine` closing tally, run against a fixture `decisions.md`, matches a mechanical count of that file's own entries by type.
- No closing-summary tally field appears outside `refine-closing-summary.md`'s documented vocabulary without that file being updated first.

## Release Note

Made backlog refine's closing tally come from its own decision log so the two can never disagree.

## Technical Approach

Add a small CLI helper — a new `hooks.js` subcommand, or a function alongside `bin/log-decision.js`'s existing `decisions.md` write path — that reads a run's `decisions.md`, classifies each line against the exact per-type templates `refine-closing-summary.md` already documents (`AUTO … set priority:…`, `AUTO … updated **Related:**…`, `AUTO … granted auto:build…`, `AUTO … flagged back…`, `AUTO … repaired dependency…`, `AUTO … stamped needs:decision…`, `AUTO … skipped …`, `FAILED …`), and prints the per-type counts in the documented tally-line format. `refine-mode.md`'s Step 5 (the closing-summary render `refine-closing-summary.md` specifies) then shells out to this helper to produce the tally line, rather than composing it from memory — turning the file's existing "no second bookkeeping channel" intent from a prose convention into an actual mechanical check. Constrain the per-type vocabulary to exactly the eight fields `refine-closing-summary.md` already documents (`priority set`, `Related updated`, `granted`, `flagged back`, `dependency-repair`, `needs-decision`, `skipped`, `failed`) — the helper's own classifier is the enforcement point: a line matching none of the eight templates should surface as a visible warning in the helper's own output rather than being silently dropped or letting the caller invent an unlisted field name. Separately, at each closing-text call site that states a specific about-to-happen action ("writing the watermark," "closing the run"), require the corresponding write call's own exit code to confirm success before that sentence renders, or omit the sentence when it didn't run.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/backlog/refine-closing-summary.md` — documents the tally vocabulary and the "counts these lines by type" convention; needs a pointer to the new mechanical helper once it exists
- `plugin/bin/log-decision.js` — candidate location for the new tally-derivation function, since it already owns the `decisions.md` write path this helper reads
- `plugin/skills/backlog/refine-mode.md` — Step 5's closing-summary render is the call site that needs to shell out to the new helper instead of hand-composing the tally

## Gotchas

- The fixture-based acceptance test needs a `decisions.md` fixture covering every one of the eight documented line types plus at least one malformed/unclassified line, to prove the helper's classifier doesn't silently drop or miscount lines it doesn't recognize.
- `collision-reconciled` (the extra field seen in the cited incident) does not appear anywhere in this repo's current skill prose (verified by grep) — this fix either needs to retire that phrase entirely from future renders, or document it in `refine-closing-summary.md` if a maintainer decides it's a legitimate addition; the Deliverables above leave that as an open documentation choice, not a foregone one.

Surface: infra

Origin: by:feedback (self-referential session evaluation, /claude-tweaks:feedback bare invocation)

**Related:** #2722

## Current State

When the same skill is invoked twice in one session, the harness itself annotates the second invocation as a re-invocation ("the skill instructions were previously loaded") — but the full `SKILL.md` body is still injected a second time, byte-identical to the first. In a session on 2026-09-20/21, `/claude-tweaks:backlog` and `/claude-tweaks:feedback` were each invoked twice; each second invocation carried the harness's own "previously loaded" annotation immediately followed by a full re-injection of that skill's `SKILL.md` (over 26KB and 35KB respectively). Separately, a reference doc citation in `_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md` names "the `resolve-run-dir` CLI" (confirmed: line 3's introductory sentence) without spelling its actual invocation form (`node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/hooks.js" resolve-run-dir`, confirmed present only later, at line 14's "Resolving it" section) — which led to guessing a nonexistent `bin/resolve-run-dir.js` path; recovering required reading that file's full ~24KB body to find the one line documenting the real invocation.

## Deliverables

- On a harness-flagged re-invocation of a skill already resident in context, consider whether the citing convention (or the harness's own skill-loading behavior, if within this plugin's control) can inject only the frontmatter/args block rather than the full body a second time.
- In `_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md` (and any other `_shared` doc that names a CLI by an informal label), spell the exact invocation form at first mention, not just in a "Resolving it" subsection a reader may not reach before guessing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A second same-session invocation of a skill the harness has already flagged as previously-loaded does not re-inject that skill's full body content.
- `_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md`'s first mention of `resolve-run-dir` names its real invocation form (`node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/hooks.js" resolve-run-dir`), so a reader does not need to reach the "Resolving it" section to avoid guessing a standalone script path.

## Release Note

Reduced the context cost of invoking a skill that is already loaded.

## Technical Approach

The two deliverables have very different scope. The doc-citation fix (second deliverable, second AC) is small and mechanical: edit `_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md`'s line 3 introductory sentence to name the actual invocation form (`node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/hooks.js" resolve-run-dir`) inline, rather than only "the `resolve-run-dir` CLI reference" — the same fix applies to any other `_shared` doc found to name a CLI informally at first mention without its invocation form. The first deliverable (skill re-injection) is a harness-behavior question, not necessarily something this plugin's own skill files can fix directly — if the harness's re-injection is structural (outside plugin control), the resolution may be "document the constraint and accept it" rather than a code change; if there IS a citing-convention lever within this plugin's control (e.g. a skill noting "if already loaded this session, skip to section X" rather than relying on the harness alone), evaluate that instead. Treat the first AC as satisfied by either a real behavior change or an explicit, justified determination that none is possible within this plugin's control.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md` — line 3's informal `resolve-run-dir` mention, to be updated with the real invocation form
- Other `_shared/*.md` files — sweep for the same "names a CLI informally at first mention" pattern while addressing this record, per the Deliverables' own "and any other `_shared` doc" scope

## Gotchas

- The first deliverable is explicitly hedged ("if within this plugin's control") — a build that concludes the harness's re-injection behavior isn't something this plugin's skill files can influence should document that conclusion and its reasoning, not force an ineffective workaround just to show activity on the AC.
- Don't conflate this record's doc-citation fix with #2722's broader lazy-load/context-overhead work (Related) — this record's second deliverable is narrowly about naming an invocation form at first mention, not about splitting or restructuring the file's sections.

## Original request

Sequential skill re-invocation re-injects the whole SKILL.md verbatim even when the harness states it's already loaded

Origin: by:feedback (self-referential session evaluation, /claude-tweaks:feedback bare invocation)

**Related:** #2722

## Current State

Separately, a reference doc citation in `_shared/pipeline-run-dir.md` names "the `resolve-run-dir` CLI" without spelling its actual invocation form (`node bin/hooks.js resolve-run-dir`), which led to guessing a nonexistent `bin/resolve-run-dir.js` path; recovering required reading that file's full ~24KB body to find the one line documenting the real invocation.
